events.legal_authority: unresolved; constitutional and police/martial-law bases require Korean instruments
later_finding: National Institute of Korean History constitutional-history account
events.finding: ROK Government announced that absent Assembly members would be guided/escorted by police. Police searched for legislators; scores spent successive nights in the Assembly Hall, and seven legislators then on trial in the alleged Communist-conspiracy case were brought in. This secured a quorum. The source supports government/police coercive attendance enforcement, but this pass does not locate a signed order naming the individual decision-maker.

proposed_by: compromise special-committee process; individual authorship unresolved
events.legal_authority: 1948 Constitution amendment procedure; procedural compliance contested in later constitutional-history account
later_finding: National Institute of Korean History constitutional-history account
events.finding: A 166-member plenary received a special-committee report combining direct election of President/Vice-President, bicameral legislature, and limited cabinet responsibility. FRUS records adoption 163-0 with 3 abstentions. NIKH's constitutional-history material separately notes coercive pressure and procedural defects, including lack of prior public announcement, so substantive passage and procedural legitimacy must remain distinct claims.

State assessed the internal crisis as resolved for the time being after passage, but had not yet received word that Pusan martial law was lifted. It also reported press censorship lifted, VOA relay restored, and Rhee ordering a new trial for the Assemblyman sentenced to death by court martial. Passage therefore did not equal instantaneous termination of all emergency/coercive measures.

Muccio reported broad relief but described the compromise as widely recognized as a Rhee victory; opposition and neutral leaders hoped martial law and restrictions would be lifted. This is diplomatic observation of political reaction, not a vote-by-vote Korean actor record.

events.finding: The Assembly passed legislation to give effect to the new constitutional provisions. Sponsor, committee path, roll call, promulgation number, and executive implementation remain open Korean-source targets.

claims.note: Quorum was secured through police escort/search and detention-like overnight presence; later NIKH account also records coercive pressure and procedural defects.
Final package combined direct presidential election/bicameralism with limited cabinet responsibility, so it should be modeled as a compromise package even though Rhee emerged politically advantaged.
US officials described political relief/resolution while still awaiting lifting of martial law and restoration of a freer atmosphere.
Current directly opened record attributes announcement/action to the ROK Government and police. A named Korean order or cabinet/Home Ministry record is still required for personal-order attribution.

supporting_evidence: formal Assembly passage recorded in doc-frus-1952-d206
claims.note: NIKH retrospective material identifies ignored procedural requirements and absence of prior public announcement, while noting legality was not openly challenged at the time. Preserve formal enactment separately from procedural-validity analysis.

adversarial_checks: Tested whether July 4 passage alone proves a free legislative bargain: police-enforced quorum evidence cuts against that simplification.
Tested whether coercion means every legislator voted under a specific threat: member-level evidence remains missing, so no such blanket inference is made.
Tested whether the final text was simply Rhee's original draft: compromise features from the Assembly side were included.
Tested whether compromise features mean Rhee did not gain politically: Muccio's July 12 reporting describes it as widely recognized as a Rhee victory.
Tested whether the political crisis ended exactly on July 4: July 9 reporting still lacked confirmation martial law was lifted.
Tested whether the July 2 police operation can be directly attributed to Rhee personally: named order remains absent in inspected material.
Tested whether formal Assembly passage settles procedural legality: NIKH retrospective account identifies procedural defects.
Tested whether the seven conspiracy defendants' attendance proves the conspiracy charge: attendance/quorum fact does not validate the charge.
Tested whether US acceptance of the compromise means approval of coercive methods: US records distinguish substantive acceptability from prior opposition to coercion.
Tested whether July 15 implementation closes the event: implementing act number, sponsors, roll call and promulgation chain remain open.

cross_provenance_bundles.note: US official synthesis explicitly cites UNCURK; Korean national-history retrospective independently flags procedural/coercive issues. Full A/2187 text and Korean Assembly minutes still needed.
Two US diplomatic records agree that relief did not immediately guarantee lifting martial law; Korean/UN source still needed.
